``` ::: ::: ::: ## QR decomposition Given $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$, QR decomposition factorizes $\mathbf{A}$ as $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{R}$. - Usually use *economy QR*, $\mathbf{Q} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times r}$ where $r$ is numerical rank. - $\mathbf{Q}$ has orthonormal columns; i.e. $\mathbf{Q}^\top \mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$ (identity matrix). - $\mathbf{R}$ has upper triangular structure (but not square in general). - Complexity: $2np^{2} - \frac{2}{3} p^{3}$ flops; $\mathbf{Q}$ is not stored and requires additional $2np^{2} - \frac{2}{3} p^{3}$ flops (Householder method) - Less numerically stable compared to other methods for linear systems. ## Gram-Schmidt Algorithm **Input**: Vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_k \in \mathbb{R}^n$. **Output**: The *Gram-Schmidt algorithm* generates a sequence of orthonormal vectors $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \ldots$. - For $i=1,\ldots,k$: 1. Orthogonalization: $\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i = \mathbf{a}_i - [(\mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_1 + \cdots + (\mathbf{q}_{i-1}' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_{i-1}]$. 2. Test for linear independence: if $\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i = \mathbf{0}$, quit. 3. Normalization: $\mathbf{q}_i = \tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i / \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i\|$. - If G-S does not stop early (in step 2), $\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_k$ are linearly independent. - If G-S stops early in iteration $i=j$, then $\mathbf{a}_j$ is a linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_{j-1}$ and $\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_{j-1}$ are linearly independent. ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Inputs a1 = [0.5, 2] a2 = [1.5, 0.5] p1 = plot([0 0; a1[1] a2[1]], [0 0; a1[2] a2[2]], arrow = true, color = :purple, axis = ([], false), legend = :none, xlims = (-2, 2), ylims = (-2, 2), annotations = [ (a1[1] + 0.2, a1[2], L"a_1"), (a2[1] + 0.2, a2[2], L"a_2") ], framestyle = :origin, aspect_ratio = :equal, title = "1" ) t = 0:0.01:2π plot!(p1, sin.(t), cos.(t), color = :gray) # orthogonalizing a1 q̃1 = copy(a1) p2 = plot([0 0; q̃1[1] a2[1]], [0 0; q̃1[2] a2[2]], arrow = true, color = [:red :purple], axis = ([], false), legend = :none, xlims = (-2, 2), ylims = (-2, 2), annotations = [ (q̃1[1] + 0.2, q̃1[2], L"\tilde{q}_1"), (a2[1] + 0.2, a2[2], L"a_2") ], framestyle = :origin, aspect_ratio = :equal, title = "2" ) t = 0:0.01:2π plot!(p2, sin.(t), cos.(t), color = :gray) # normalizing q̃1 q1 = q̃1 / norm(q̃1) p3 = plot([0 0; ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (norm(q1), norm(q2), norm(q3)) = (1.0, 1.0, 0.9999999999999999) q1' * q2 = 2.4203152163668796e-16 q1' * q3 = -1.2856358646856095e-16 q2' * q3 = -9.185840984983169e-18 ``` ::: ::: ## Complexity Computational complexity of G-S algorithm: - Step 1 of iteration $i$ requires (1) $i-1$ inner products, $\mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_i, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{i-1}' \mathbf{a}_i$, which costs $(i-1)(2n-1)$ flops, and (2) $2n(i-1)$ flops to compute $\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i$. - Step 2 of iteration $i$ requires less than $n$ flops. - Step 3 of iteration $i$ requires $3n$ flops to normalize $\|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i\|$. - Assuming no early termination, total computational cost of the GS algorithm to orthonormalize a set of $k$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is: $$ \sum_{i=1}^k [(4n-1) (i - 1) + 3n] = (4n - 1) \frac{k(k-1)}{2} + 3nk \approx 2nk^2 = O(nk^2), $$ using $\sum_{i=1}^k (i - 1) = k(k-1)/2$. ## GS Algorithm and QR Factorization The operations in GS can be compactly expressed as $$ \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{R}, $$ where $\mathbf{A} = (\mathbf{a}_1 \, \cdots \, \mathbf{a}_k) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$, $\mathbf{Q} = (\mathbf{q}_1 \, \cdots \, \mathbf{q}_k) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$ satisfying $\mathbf{Q}'\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}_k$ ($\mathbf{Q}$ has orthonormal columns), and $\mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}$ is an upper triangular matrix with positive diagonal elements. What are the entries in $\mathbf{R}$? In the $i$-th iteration of the Gram-Schmidt algorithm \begin{eqnarray*} \text{Orthogonalization step: } & & \tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i = \mathbf{a}_i - (\mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_1 - \cdots - (\mathbf{q}_{i-1}' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_{i-1} \\ \text{Normalization step: } & & \mathbf{q}_i = \tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i / \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i\|. \end{eqnarray*} Therefore, $$ \mathbf{a}_i = (\mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_1 + \cdots + (\mathbf{q}_{i-1}' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_{i-1} + \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i\| \mathbf{q}_i. $$ This tells us $R_{ij} = \mathbf{q}_i' \mathbf{a}_j$ for $i < j$ and $R_{ii} = \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i\|$. Thus overall Gram-Schmidt algorithm performs $$ \mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} | & | & & | & | \\ \mathbf{a}_1 & \mathbf{a}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf{a}_{k-1} & \mathbf{a}_k \\ | & | & & | & | \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} | & | & & | & | \\ \mathbf{q}_1 & \mathbf{q}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf{q}_{k-1} & \mathbf{q}_k \\ | & | & & | & | \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_1\| & \mathbf{q}_1'\mathbf{a}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_{k-1} & \mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_k \\ & \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_2\| & \cdots & \mathbf{q}_2' \mathbf{a}_{k-1} & \mathbf{q}_2' \mathbf{a}_k \\ & & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\ & & & \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_{k-1}\| & \mathbf{q}_{k-1}' \mathbf{a}_k \\ & & & & \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_k\| \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{R}. $$ ::: {.callout-warning} The Gram-Schmidt algorithm is **numerically unstable**. The specific issue that arises is that the basis vectors $\mathbf{q}_{k}$ may lose their orthogonality. The [*modified* Gram-Schmidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gram%E2%80%93Schmidt_process#Numerical_stability) is preferred. In your homework you will implement QR via Householder reflections, which is more stable and efficient (the basis vectors are computed implicitly). ::: ## Solving linear systems Now look at solving linear systems (full column rank), assuming we already have $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{R}$: $$ \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} \equiv \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} \implies \text{Solve}~\mathbf{R} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{Q}^\top \mathbf{y} $$ - Form RHS: $2np$ flops (since $\mathbf{Q}$ is $n \times p$) - Solve with backward substitution: $p^{2}$ flops - Total: $2np + p^{2}$ ## Solving least squares Least squares problem $\min_{\beta}~\frac{1}{2} \|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\beta\|_{2}^{2}$ has the same complexity: - **Why?** Use properties of orthonormal matrices... - Reduction to $\min_{\beta}~\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{Q}^\top \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{R}\beta\|_{2}^{2}$. - **Fit $\beta$** (QR + solve): $2(n-1)p^{2} - \frac{2}{3} p^{3} + 2np$ - **Standard errors for estimates**: Requires inverting $\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}$ (one of a few cases where it is acceptable!) We can be far more clever about inverting the matrix. View the problem of computing $(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X})^{-1}$ as: $$ \text{Solve}~\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X} \mathbf{\Sigma} = \mathbf{I} \quad \equiv \quad \mathbf{R}^\top \mathbf{R} \mathbf{\Sigma} = \mathbf{I}; $$ that is, we solve two triangular systems for the matrix-valued variable $\mathbf{\Sigma}$. ::: {.callout-note} Note that $\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\beta})$ depends on $\mathbf{X}$ in linear regression, but the explicit form for the standard errors depends on whatever assumptions we are willing to make about the random component (e.g. normal errors). ::: ## Example: Longley data ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} column_labels = ["Employed", "Price", "GNP", "Jobless", "Military", "PopSize", "Year"] longley = CSV.read(joinpath("assets", "longley.txt"), DataFrame; header = column_labels, delim = ' ', ignorerepeated = true ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
